#3348. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

The Reebok Nano X5 cross training shoe made it into our line-up for being the best in the Nano series yet. It steers away from the more aggressive Nano X4 design and toward a shoe we’d choose for lifting and HIIT.

The sturdy design might have Olympic lifters rejoicing, but for anyone running a distance, I'd shop elsewhere.

#3346. Report: John Ternus pushing Craig Federighi to speed up Apple software engineering

In the past few years, a major Apple story (especially in the age of AI) has been that the company isn’t moving fast enough in the space to keep up with competitors. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, new Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing on software chief Craig Federighi to ‘accelerate’ Apple’s roadmap for software.

At the moment, there’s no indication that Apple’s well known software SVP Craig Federighi will be leaving the company. In fact, Craig has made it a very low priority of his to develop a succession plan in any sense, per Mark Gurman. That said, Ternus still wants to see change in how Craig Federighi thinks about Apple’s software strategy:

In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri.

A large part of Federighi’s approach has been how hands-on he is, resulting in his viewpoint shaping how Apple’s software development goes to a large extent. That’s left team members feeling that they have ‘limited influence’ over what happens:

Federighi is known for taking an especially hands-on role in meetings and major decisions, with some employees describing a management style that can leave little room for competing ideas to gain traction. He is also known for vigorously debating opposing viewpoints, using his command of technical details and ability to argue his position to push back against proposals he disagrees with. That approach has at times frustrated members of the software engineering and design teams, some of whom believe they have limited influence over the direction of products.

Another part is that Federighi reportedly only plans for a 12-18 month timeframe, versus the years-long roadmaps used in hardware engineering. These are some of the gaps that Apple may want to bridge in the coming years.

Separately, Vision Pro and Siri AI leader Mike Rockwell is still seriously considering stepping down. He’s currently vice president of Siri engineering:

The management concerns go beyond Federighi. Mike Rockwell, who created the Vision Pro headset in addition to leading the development of Siri AI, continues to seriously consider stepping down. That could mean leaving his role as vice president of Siri engineering — or Apple altogether — next year. Such a move would be a major blow, given his role in bringing the new Siri to market after an embarrassing two-year delay.

Interesting timing on this article. I’m sitting here with two laptops: one running Tahoe and the other one running Golden Gate, both of them full of bugs and issues that should’ve never been released outside of Apple, and thinking how great Apple’s hardware is, but how terrible their software has become. I don’t know the inner workings of Apple, so I’ve never wanted to outright blame Federighi, but given that he’s at the top of the software ladder, I can only think that he’s most likely the problem. For all I know he could be holding it altogether, but then I read something like this and makes me think that it might be time for him to go.

I don’t know about accelerating their software, I feel like their software has felt rushed and unfinished for the last 10 years or so, and increasingly so each year, but I think what the article really means is speed up the advancement in the AI aspect of Apple’s software, not actually rushing out their software in general.

In the same report, Gurman also reported that Apple is experimenting with a new development pipeline, giving engineers 50% more time to code and explore more, and spend less time on integration, as coding agents have improved.

It remains to be seen what else might change at Apple to enable faster development timelines, though it seems likely that Craig Federighi may have to release his ‘firm grip’ on the software engineering org, and instead allow some other leaders to blossom and act on their own accord.

#3345. Netflix Refuses To Remove Russell Brand Stand-Up Special Featuring Crude Sex Joke

Netflix will continue to stream a Russell Brand stand-up special after the comedian was convicted of rape and sexual assault.

Russell Brand: Re:Birth, the 2018 original comedy show filmed in front of a live audience at the Hackney Empire in East London, will not be removed following internal discussions at the streamer.

During the special, Brand references his sexual escapades while reflecting on how long it took to conceive his first child with wife, Laura Brand, who is thanked in the credits.

“I’ve hardly been conservative with sperm. Giving the stuff away like sticky confetti,” he said. “The real miracle is that one of them’s been allowed to germinate instead of being squandered in a stranger’s eyelashes.” Related Stories News Jonathan Ross Explains Backstory Behind "Tasteless" David Walliams Joke News 'The Age Of Innocence' Sets Netflix Release Date; First Photos Of Camila Morrone, Kristine Froseth & Ben Radcliffe

Commenting on the birth of his daughter, he added that “there ain’t nothing like seeing a vagina coming out of a vagina to make you re-evaluate your attitude towards people with vaginas.” Watch on Deadline

Netflix will continue to host Russell Brand: Re:Birth but will no longer actively promote the show to members after Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday.

Russell Brand: Re:Birth will not feature in Netflix viewing recommendations and does not appear when searching Brand’s name. The show can be found, however, by searching for “British stand-up comedy.”

A Netflix source said: “We prioritize choice and control for our members: the freedom to watch what, how and when you want, with recommendations and ratings to inform those choices.”

Netflix has a high bar for content removals. The streamer has stood by Dave Chappelle over his views on transgender rights, while in 2022, the streamer rebuffed calls to take down Jimmy Carr’s 2022 special His Dark Material amid a backlash over a joke about the Gypsy, Roma, and Traveller community.

Brand was last week found guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison.

In sentencing remarks following the four-week trial, Mr Justice Bennathan described Brand as a “sexual predator,” and said his fame protected him until 2023, when Channel 4 and The Times of London published allegations about his conduct.

The judge paid tribute to the “determination and bravery” of the women who made complaints about Brand. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say ‘no’ and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” Bennathan said.

#3344. The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For

Editor’s note: This article contains major spoilers for the documentary “You Can See Everything.”

This is a joke offered by one of three people on a Zoom with Rolling Stone one October afternoon. Because like virtually everybody who’s been to the movies in the past month, and even many who haven’t, the subject these three are most keen to chat about is the brain-boggling, meme-launching, WTF-did-I-just-watch documentary You Can See Everything.

If you haven’t seen it yet, you undoubtedly know the elevator pitch: Nathan Fielder embeds himself in the home of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, right before Holmes reports to prison. You also know the major conversation-starter moments: The shower scene. The egg-whipping. The abundant close-ups of unblinking stares.

The one thing that makes this virtual coffee klatch a little different is that the folks ready to discuss the ins and outs of this cultural phenomenon include Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim. And if you’re among the many, many folks who’ve helped turn this gonzo experiment in nonfiction filmmaking into a blockbuster, you can likely guess who the third person in the chat might be. Hint: It’s not Holmes.

Rather, it’s the woman who’s played her not once, but now twice — Amanda Seyfried, the Dropout star whose presence in the documentary’s second half has been one of the best-kept moviegoing secrets in recent memory, and the aspect that sends it into a whole new stratosphere of mind-fuckery.

Seyfried joined her co-conspirators for an exclusive conversation — her first time on the record about the film, and the first time the three collaborators have discussed it since the premiere — to talk about how she was drawn into the project, that awkward on-camera phone call with Holmes, and how they’ve all been processing the experience. Making and releasing the film has been an emotional roller coaster for each of them (Oppenheim says it “made my brain and body feel on fire”), but Seyfried, for one, has enjoyed the ride.

“I have no regrets,” she says. “I’m having the time of my life right now!” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.Oppenheim: Well, where should we start?

Seyfried: My first question is: What am I doing here? What am I doing in this movie? How did I get here?

Fielder: That’s a great question, Amanda. How did you get here?

Oppenheim: I feel like there was a certain point in the process of making this where we wanted to expand the bubble [of people involved in the project]. But so many of the people we reached out to didn’t want to be on camera because Elizabeth had this toxic reputation.Fielder: This was two years after we had shot in that beach house with them. We were just like, “Where do we go next?” The Dropout kept coming up. Elizabeth’s parents really had very strong feelings about it, and they felt it was one of the main ways the general public knew about who Elizabeth Holmes was. So we thought it would be interesting to talk to you.

I got your phone number through Emma Stone. We had a 30-minute Zoom, and you were like, “Yeah, come over with cameras.” We wanted to show you what became the first half of the film, and then we would talk about it. That’s all you agreed to. Related Content ‘SNL’: Druski Impersonates ‘Crazy’ Elizabeth Holmes in Meta-Documentary Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Haven't Seen Enough? The Books and Shows to Read and Watch After 'You Can See Everything' Watch Amanda Seyfried’s Joni Mitchell Cover Get Interrupted by Ghostface

The crazy thing to me [was that] you didn’t go through any talent reps or anyone. You just said, “Yeah, come over!” Why did you trust us like that?

Seyfried: I remember when [Emma] texted, and I was like, “Nathan Fielder? Ooh, I wonder if he wants to make something with me?”

My sister is a big fan [of yours, Nathan], and I know a lot of people are big fans of Nathan for You. I’d only seen The Curse. When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, “Oh, he just wants some advice. He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed.” After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed. It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening.

“It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings.”

Seyfried: I wasn’t nervous. There were just way more people than I expected coming into my apartment [laughs]. I had just gotten back from the Venice Film Festival, and I said this is the only time I can do it; I’m just never in the city. I didn’t know how long it was going to take. I thought, “Wait a minute, there’s cameras. I should probably put on some mascara …” There was no protection. There was no advocate for me. I just felt like I was totally game because I was so invested in what you were doing, and already had this strange level of trust in you guys.

Fielder: It’s not dissimilar to Elizabeth, I guess, who also just had a strange level of trust.

Seyfried: Not dissimilar … but not super similar, I would say.

Seyfried: I would say there was a lot of risk in the back of my head, and then when I told my agent and lawyer that I had already done it? Not the normal process [laughs]. But I go off and do my own thing sometimes, and nobody had any say or control over what I was doing with Nathan and Lance. My lawyer was like, “Well, now we have to retroactively set your deal in place because you need protection.” We weren’t even considering reenactments at that point.

Fielder: We should clarify that because, yeah, all you’d agreed to was just coming in, and we’d show you the stuff and talk.

Seyfried: I wasn’t even a subject at that point.Oppenheim: I think you said that you’d never play this person again. When we started showing you that stuff — there was a moment in the conversation where you started imitating her on camera, and you gave Nathan this look. What brought you back into that?Seyfried: Muscle memory. I think the reason I was able to capture my version of Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout was not her Nightline interview, or 60 Minutes, or whatever footage I’d seen. It was the 10 hours of deposition tapes, where she was present and completely consistent. That’s the thing that my brain is locked into. So even though it had been a bunch of years, I see her again in the footage … and I can’t help but tilt my head a little bit. It’s muscle memory when you play a character as intensely as I did for as long as I did. I do think there’s something almost uncontrollable. When I was talking to you, it was already coming out of me in some way.

“It wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies.”

Fielder: You started doing it, but you never actually said you would play her again. It’s so interesting, because the process of making this was to try to give as much information as we could to the audience on how we interpreted these moments that were happening in the house and with her. Anything that didn’t happen on camera, we took notes of. But we were talking about the oddness of these early meetings, and we always assumed that, well, obviously these things can’t be part of the film. But then we were sort of like, “Wait, would the idea of doing a re-creation work?” At first we didn’t even consider it because we thought it was a little lame, maybe, to do these types of things. But the way you engaged with it when we shot at your apartment, it felt to us like there was something in you. It was like you wanted to revisit it.

Oppenheim: It felt like you had unfinished business — like it was pouring out of you. You were unresolved or something.

Fielder: Did you have something unresolved?

Seyfried: Don’t we all? [Laughs.] I mean, now that people have seen the movie, isn’t everybody kind of feeling that? That’s the thing about how powerful this whole project is, the nuance of it and its capacity to be all things. You can’t resolve any of it. You can learn about how you feel and you can learn about your perspective on things, but …

It’s not that I was unresolved; it’s that I had more information now because of [your] footage. Anybody who’s watched this documentary knows that the first 90 [minutes] or so, there’s a lot of information there. So the idea that I could go on this journey with you guys, however you needed me, in whatever capacity, was very interesting to me.

Fielder: We started having conversations about: “OK, would you portray her again?” All I said was that we’d want you to re-create some initial conversations that happened off-camera. But then we also said, because this is a documentary, we didn’t want to discuss these scenes or show you scripts in advance. We just want you to show up, and we’ll talk about the scenes on camera. Anything that comes up in those conversations will potentially be part of it. People should know that you had no creative control over this project. Anything that was filmed—

Fielder: You had no approval over anything. You were just engaging with these scenes for the first time. Were you nervous at any point during this?

Seyfried: Yes! I mean, there was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything was scary, but I still had that drive that was more in the front seat — which was the literal front seat with you in the car. I was just like, “Let’s go, buddy! I want to put my hand in the fire!”

Fielder: We just had planned to do those first few re-creations, the meeting and the one at the house. Nothing beyond that. And then you were getting drawn in, and it seemed like you had to go to Billy. You’re now in this process, and it’s not like we can drive this thing forward because so much is based on your comfort level. What made you want to keep going beyond those re-creations?

Seyfried: I don’t know. I don’t know. It’s the same as whatever was driving you guys this whole time.Fielder: Why did you want to meet Billy?

Seyfried: I just … [pauses]. It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me. I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.

You wanted that, too, but it had to come from me because I don’t think you would have put me in that position. I did feel protected by you guys pretty early on. I felt like I trusted you. Even though I kept jokingly saying, “You’re not going to ruin my life, right?”

Fielder: And what was my answer? I forget.

Seyfried: “I’m not trying to. But maybe.” [Laughs.] Just kidding.

Fielder: That sounds like what I would say, actually.

Oppenheim: It was such a gigantic leap of faith. I don’t know if you know how amazing and also how insane it was that you were willing to put yourself out there in this way.

Seyfried: But I want people to know that it wasn’t like I jumped into the deep end. It was a process. “What are you doing on this date?” “I don’t know. I’m busy on this date, but I’m around on this date?” “OK, let’s meet here.” So it was just a step-by-step process. It wasn’t like a script, and we were going to shoot it. I wasn’t committing to shooting a movie. I was committing to each event or moment, and those are little leaps of faith that ended up feeling bigger.

Oppenheim: If you’re saying you’re a “Billy detective,” what did you feel after you met him? Did your feelings change at all?

Seyfried: Nothing changed. It only got worse. That’s very clear in the doc, I think.

Fielder: Did you feel like, “Oh, he’s different?” Or were you like, “He’s the same guy I saw in that footage?”

Seyfried: I had to put on a different hat [when I met him]. I was filtered. I wouldn’t necessarily call it acting, but … I was thinking about how I wanted to protect myself, but I also wanted to give the guy a chance to be as he is. I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children — with their children. I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of shit about him up until that point.

Because look, I do not like him. But I’m coming into this man’s house. I just wanted to be a presence, the way that you guys are so good at being present in these situations. But you also knew him. The whole crew knew him, and he knew them. Billy doesn’t know me at all. He just assumes many things about me, which is normal.

So I’m just trying to engage with him, and it’s fine. It’s going fine. And then [Elizabeth] calls, and that was just … what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least. Everything I’m feeling, you can see. I don’t even have to describe it to you.

“The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy.”

Fielder: I want people to know that everything that’s outside of the scripted reenactments, like that phone call, that’s all coming from you — we’re not saying, “Well, you have to say this or that” in any of these things. This is all just happening in real time.

Seyfried: We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. And I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls, and … Someone asked me if that was real, if that was really her on the phone. And I’m like, “It’s a documentary. Who else would it be?”

Oppenheim: Every time I watch the movie, it feels like your performance in the reenactments evolves, from that first one to the final one.

Seyfried: From insecurity to … um, security. [Laughs.]

Oppenheim: Did anything change over the course of it? Was it something in the way you prepared, or did experiencing all the stuff you did with us impact anything?

Seyfried: I think it had to do with intensity. I mean, that last scene in the prison is all from Nathan’s memory. [To Nathan] You did an amazing job trying to remember everything.

Fielder: The second I got out [of the visiting room], I recorded everything I could remember into my phone.

Seyfried: You did your due diligence with that. I think the stakes were so high at that point for all of us because it had just happened. The reenactments I was doing from the beginning … [they] were things that had happened when you were with them years prior. I was still insecure about it, and I was like, “I don’t know if I can still do the voice.” Also, the audience will have just seen her for 90 minutes — how are they gonna just suspend disbelief? It was very much like, “How am I going to do this? I don’t know if I can capture her anymore.”And then by the end, I had been doing it enough, and I really had a good time in the pizza house doing the A24 meeting [where we show Billy negotiating for movie profits]. I really got my stride, and then the stakes were so high because you had literally just gone to the prison. For most of the filming, we were like, “When are you gonna go? When can you go?”

Fielder: We were really focused on trying to get cameras in there because it was really frustrating to have these things that kept happening off-camera that were so relevant to our understanding. We were hopeful for a time that we could get cameras in there, but … I mean, you see it a little bit in the movie where I wasn’t excited about doing a re-creation of that final visit. Also, there was a rumor online that I had visited her before. That is bad information. I had never visited her in prison before that one [time] in the film. So, just to clarify that.

Anyway, I was nervous about re-creating that because the earlier re-creations were more about describing what happened in the house and in those early meetings. This one was: I’m asking her questions, and the way she responds and the expression on her face is what would be telling [the audience] about it. I was really skeptical that those things could be captured in a re-creation without it feeling goofy, or just, like, so detached from reality. It was the best we could do given all the constraints on access to her.

But then — and I don’t know if I ever told you this, Amanda — but it wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies. Because when anything was slightly off in what you were doing, we would talk about it. It was really like, “This is not how it was.”Seyfried: You were so specific.

Fielder: But when you got it, it was like, “Wow. This is it. This is what I experienced.” I never thought that would be possible in a re-creation. Really, it’s a testament to your performance. You came in with choices that you were making as a performer, which is great. But sometimes it would be off from what I had witnessed, and so we’d adjust until we got it right, and then it was incredible when you hit it. Even the way you responded to the questions when it was, like, almost nonanswers and certain things, it’s exactly how she answered.

Seyfried: Do you remember when we were in the barn and you were telling me I was doing it wrong? I remember that at one point I’m like, “How was it done, Nathan??”

Oppenheim: There’s an amazing expression on your face where it’s like, “Come on, man, which way is it?”

The performance you’re doing here — even though you’ve done the character before, it feels different than anything else you’ve ever done. I remember being behind the monitor for the final reenactment, and I did feel like I was seeing her. It was startling.

Seyfried: How did you edit together, like, 700 hours of footage? There could have been 1,000 versions of this movie.

“I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls!”

Oppenheim: This happened when we were shooting, but especially when we were in the edit room with Adam Locke-Norton — who’s edited a lot of Nathan’s stuff — we would gravitate toward the moments that we most disagreed on.

Fielder: “Disagreed on” in terms of what we were witnessing.Oppenheim: Right, the moments that provided the most cognitive dissonance. Our experience watching them would be so different from one another’s, and that felt like a powder keg or something.

Fielder: People are not, you know, normally this difficult for us to make sense of.Seyfried: Well, normally people answer a question. She doesn’t answer questions.

Oppenheim: She’s like a human optical illusion or something.Seyfried: A David Blaine trick.Oppenheim: [Laughs.] Yeah! A couple weeks ago, I asked Adam, “Do you feel that if someone saw all 700 hours, they would come away with a different conclusion — or different conclusions — than just watching the three-hour film?” And he said, “Actually, I don’t think so.” I just thought that was so telling that it’s like, wow, it’s not always the more you know about someone, the more you see someone. There had already been so much [coverage of] her case. The documentary, the book, the podcast …

Oppenheim: We wanted to do something that was forward-looking and not just regurgitating stuff that was already in the public record or had been extensively reported on.

Fielder: So, Amanda, when you arrived on the re-creation sets, it seemed like you were curious about what objects were in the real locations versus choices our set decorators or production design team made. Why was that something that interested you?

Seyfried: I think I was just grasping at anything that could ground me back into this world because it had been so long, and I think I was also experiencing some kind of weird, like, meta-vortex because I had just seen Elizabeth Holmes in this house, and the house is so specific …

Oppenheim: Like you’d somehow walked into the documentary.Seyfried: Yes! That’s it! It’s like if they still had the set of Family Matters up, and I walked onto the set. You become a part of what you’ve experienced in a way that you don’t get to do very often. Nobody had been [in Holmes and Evans’ beach house] for two years or whatever. And suddenly it’s like I’ve time-traveled two years into the past.

Fielder: It felt like you were stepping into our memories, in a way, and we wanted to capture that feeling of memory in the edit. Like [the audience was] transitioning from the first half [of the film] into these re-creations.

Seyfried: The way you shot it, who’s in it, the questions you asked, the way you lived inside this process — people cannot stop talking about it for a reason. So it was that much more intense for me when I walked in, because it was like she had just been there. The first moment — well, besides Billy in the shower — the first moment that stuck out to me when I was watching the footage in my apartment was him grabbing the eggs. You were like, “Feel free to stop whenever you want to ask me a question.” And when the egg moment happened, I immediately hit the space bar [to stop the video], and I was like, “What the fuck?” And you were like—Fielder: “Yeah! I know!”Seyfried: So, like, these moments, like, this experience that I had watching it — I’m now in that same space. It’s just crazy. It’s great for an actor. But it’s just weird for me.

Oppenheim: The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy.

Seyfried: Same!Oppenheim: What was going on in your head?

Seyfried: I was honestly trying to connect with him. We were all sitting there eating really good Chinese food, and, obviously, there were questions we wanted to ask. But for me, since I’m not an interviewer or an investigator, I’m not so good at asking questions and getting the timing right. And Nathan, you had a rapport with him. I was still creating this rapport. Plus, I’m in this man’s house with his kids. Did I say that earlier?

Oppenheim: You did. But I’m curious. Like when the conversation started to turn … I’m just behind the camera thinking, “What is going on?”

Seyfried: There was no reason for him to get that aggressive. [Pauses.] That’s the word I’m going to use, as it’s more diplomatic. If my jaw wasn’t obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged. I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, “Oh, I don’t think so, buddy.” I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, “OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things. I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s “building monuments of love” to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her. And not only am I protective of myself, I’m just trying to set the record straight in a way where I’m trying to defend myself, too, while maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn’t kick us out, you know?

Oppenheim: I don’t have any memory of you saying, like, “Can we cut that out?” or anything like that.

Seyfried: I’m a people pleaser [laughs]. I think a lot of my friends who knew that I was doing this secret project were like, “Are you sure you’re OK? Are you sure you want to keep doing this?” And I was like, “Yeah, it feels like sure … maybe … I don’t know?” There was never a point at which I was just going to be like, “You know what? Let’s not do this.” I did get close to being like, “No reenactments. That just seems weird. That just seems like going back to the well, and it might be dry.” But the truth is, we all kept this idea alive.

I joined you both way later on. But I also feel like each of us has brought something very specific to this project. And when you needed me, I came because of how invested you were, and how I felt like we were all on the same page at a point. We were like a band. We were like a team. It felt like part of the team. And when I felt part of the team, it made me want to go even further. It’s not necessarily about being safe, but about doing something different. And it’s not just about doing something different, but doing something that confuses you and excites you and terrifies you. That’s the shit that we have to remind each other to commit to in order to create something so wild.

Oppenheim: Every time I watch it, I feel so overwhelmed by it all. I not only feel like I’ve been taken back in time to the place where it all happened, but I feel overwhelmed by some moment that I find really funny, or some moments I find extremely sad. To me, it was important to have that range. The more we could express the emotional experience we had with them in making the film, the more I thought the film would be successful at communicating something honest.

Fielder: Amanda, would you ever do something like this again, or do you regret it?

Seyfried: What are you talking about? I don’t regret it at all. I’m having the time of my life right now! I mean, I’m not going to do this again. But neither are you!

Fielder and Oppenheim: Grooming by Jennifer Brent at Forward Artists using 111SKIN. Seyfried: Hair by Orlando Pita. Makeup by Genevieve Herr.

#3343. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3342. macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

In its blog post, Apple announced that apps will require “very explicit user action” to have Full Disk Access on your Mac. At the time of the announcement, Apple didn’t make it super clear what that would actually mean. Now, we have an idea of what’s to come.

Code sifter pdfu posted on X that Apple will be getting rid of a clever loophole that developers could use to make it easier for users to enable Full Disk Access. In current versions of macOS, if an app requests a file that would require Full Disk Access, the system denies the request and logs the app as an option in the Settings app for enabling Full Disk Access.

At that point, developers often prompt users to open that section of the Settings app and flip the toggle.

Starting as soon as macOS 27.3, apps that request files outside of the permission scope will no longer get logged, and as a result, won’t show up as an option for quickly toggling Full Disk Access, per leaker pdfu.

macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb

At the moment, developers can still request users to drag an app icon to the Settings panel to enable Full Disk Access, even once the feature flag for the aforementioned change is enabled. To me, it still doesn’t quite feel like you’ll need “very explicit user action” to enable Full Disk Access, but it’s possible this will change in the future. This is all still in development.

All in all, I’m not fully convinced that this solves the core problem. Developers are requesting Full Disk Access because they’d like to tap into things like iMessage, and there hasn’t been a better way of doing so. As long as that demand is there, users will likely still have to enable Full Disk Access and risk all sorts of other data, just so they can share their texts with an agent.

Granted, pdfu also mentions the idea of Private Folders, which could potentially allow users to grant scoped access to just the iMessage database folder. It’s unclear if that’ll be possible since there’s little detail on how Private Folders will work. If that’s the case, then hopefully Full Disk Access can stop being the default permission you have to provide for any personal data.

#3340. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3338. Trump Gloats as Republicans Kill Bid to Impeach Pete Hegseth

Pete Hegseth has dodged impeachment — for now.

Republicans in the House of Representatives successfully blocked an effort to impeach the Secretary of Defense on Tuesday night, amid a controversial, chaotic run as one of Donald Trump’s most loyal Cabinet members, highlighted by a disastrous, still-ongoing war of choice against Iran.

The House voted 211-204 to move the impeachment resolution to committee, where Republicans, who for the rest of the year control the chamber’s committees, can leave it to languish. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, potentially depriving the party of a huge win coming off of the midterm elections. The absent Democrats were: Reps. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Lou Correa (D-Calif.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Jonathan ackson (D-Ill.), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.), and Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.).

Axios reported that several Democrats who missed the vote were unable to make it because they were attending an Elect Democratic Women event and got stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on their way to the Capitol.

Hegseth would have been the second Secretary of Defense (or War) to be impeached and third Cabinet member in history to be impeached, after Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876 and Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been a thorn in the Trump administration’s side throughout his second term in office, brought articles of impeachment to Congress almost immediately after the midterm elections. The Department of Defense, meanwhile, posted an AI-generated image of Massie in tears.

#3335. Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds

Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent.

Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously …

Rossmann is a repair technician who specializes in component-level logic board repairs and data recovery. He later became a key figure in advocating for right-to-repair legislation, which Apple initially opposed and later backed.

In a recent video, he claimed that some Apple store staff were signing up customers to trials of paid services subscriptions without their informed consent. Targets set by Apple are said to have encouraged the practice.

Customers accepting the offer of a personalized shopping experience could be shown the free trials of Apple services available to them based on their recent purchases. For example, buying an iPhone currently entitles you to a free three-month subscription to Apple TV. However, these trials automatically start debiting your payment method if you don’t cancel them before they end.

Staff were instructed to show these offers to customers and were allegedly set a 40% sign-up target, which Apple tracked as a performance metric. Crucially, the offers are shown on the employee’s device rather than on the customer’s phone. A store member told Rossman that some staff were hitting the Accept button without properly obtaining consent from customers in order to hit their target.

When I asked whether they’d seen a specialist press Agree with their own eyes, they answered “Yes, I saw some specialists press on behalf of the customer. So, they are hitting agree. They are signing the customer up to something without actually having the customer click okay, hit okay, or provide express consent.”

The store member also claimed that staff were describing the offer as a gift, which further disguised the fact that it would turn into a paid recurring subscription unless canceled.

This is not shocking to me. Apple started pushing subscriptions during the sales process years ago when I worked in the stores.

I remember this being a major shift from being more customer focused over to becoming a battleground of a sales floor trying to get your "numbers". I even recall hearing that someone got promoted because their numbers were "so good" while we all knew they were signing people for AC+ without their knowledge. Sad days.

At the time of writing, Apple has not responded directly to the accusations, but in a follow-up video yesterday Rossman cites a staff member describing the company’s response.

He says a memo was read out in the morning meeting stating that only customers could press the Accept button, and internal systems indicate Apple is no longer grading staff on the signup metric.

We have reached out to Apple for comment and will update with any response.

#3333. Teens and parents can expect Instagram notifications about AI age estimation

Meta says it’s expanding its AI age estimation globally to automatically extend Instagram account protections to millions more teenagers. It says parents in the US can also expect to receive notifications later this month …

Instagram has a number of protections for the accounts of teenagers, but it’s very common for teens to lie about their age in order to circumvent them. Back in May, the company said it would be using AI-powered age estimation to address the problem.

The company said it would use the tool to block users aged below 13, and to ensure that those in the 13 to 17 range had limited accounts. Teen accounts have age-appropriate feeds, limitations on who can interact with them, and default time management tools – though things didn’t get off to the best of starts when a 12-year-old kid fooled it by using an eyebrow pencil to draw a fake moustache.

Meta today says that it is rolling out the (hopefully now eyebrow pencil-proof) tech globally.

We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.

The company goes on to say that parents in the US will receive a notification sometime this month, with a link to a video and an article about the system.

This month, parents in the United States will begin to see an in-feed video on Instagram explaining our approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article, written by Larry Magid, internet safety advocate and President and CEO of ConnectSafely, detailing our multi-layered age assurance approach, which includes keeping children under 13 off our platforms, providing age appropriate experiences for teens, and informing parents about ways they can partner with us to ensure their teens provide the correct age online.

If you don’t want to wait, you can read the article here.

Meta says the same protections will be rolled out to Threads and Facebook, although I would have thought being on Facebook in the first place is proof that it’s been a while since you were a teenager …

#3332. Rising Star Molly McCann On Finding Her Place In Panem For ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’

Molly McCann has a lot to be excited about. The 15-year-old Irish actress has already built up a roster of credits including Bad Sisters and 2020 Sundance hit title Herself, but now she’s gearing up for her biggest project to date with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate’s latest return to Suzanne Collins’ hugely popular dystopian universe.

McCann plays Louella McCoy, one of the female tributes from District 12 and a close ally of Haymitch, in a story set some 24 years before Katniss Everdeen’s story, the character famously played by Jennifer Lawrence more than a decade ago. Related Stories News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Getting Hot With $80M+ Opening Floor, Presales Ahead Of 'Wicked' - Box Office Update News Lionsgate & 3 Arts Set New Horror Banner Render Road Led By Luke Maxwell & Will Rowbotham - The Dish

“The hardest part for me was having to keep it a secret for a month,” McCann tells Deadline via Zoom from her family home in Dublin. “I just wanted to tell everyone.” Watch on Deadline

Sunrise on the Reaping, which bows worldwide on November 20, opens on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, when the Capitol demands twice the number of tributes – 48 children instead of 24. The story focuses on 16-year-old Haymitch, played by Joseph Zada, a clever and resourceful boy from District 12. (Woody Harrelson played an older Haymitch in the previous films.) Louella, who comes from the same district, and Haymitch are particularly close as they navigate their calling to the Hunger Games.

“Haymitch and Louella have such a special bond together and I think that Joe and I did a good job of recreating that and using the book to help us capture how close they were on screen,” she says.

The film boasts a stellar cast that also includes Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons and Glenn Close. Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, who played Peeta in the previous films, are also expected to return in a scene where an older Haymitch recounts his Hunger Game to them.

In the book’s epilogue, an older Haymitch notes that a young Katniss reminded him of Louella not only because of the two braids in her hair but also because of her “tough and smart” demeanor. “He calls them both sweetheart and says they look alike,” she says, adding that many of her friends kept asking her if she was playing a younger Katniss. “I was like, ‘not quite, no.’ They got so confused.”

And while McCann’s didn’t cross paths with Lawrence on set, she’s hopeful the star will enjoy her performance. “I think it’s really special that I get to share something like this with someone as incredible as Jennifer Lawrence,” she says.

McCann has been exposed to the acting world all her life. Her parents are both actors and her mother runs a stage school. This upbringing, she says, means she’s been comfortable on set from a very young age.

At the age of five, she was cast as one of the child actors in 2018 drama Rosie with Bad Sisters star Sarah Greene. A few years later McCann earned an Irish Film and Television (IFTA) nomination for Best Actress in a Supporting Role in Herself, which starred Claire Dunne and Harriet Walter. That Phyllida Lloyd-directed drama saw McCann play the daughter of a single mother (Dunne) who, after escaping an abusive partner, aims to rebuild her life in a unique manner.

Working with Lloyd, she says, was a formative experience. “She was such an amazing director and Harriet Walter is a legend. It was a great learning curve for me.”

McCann auditioned for Sunrise on the Reaping in early 2025, having only watched the original Hunger Games movies a few months earlier and she admits that she was unaware of how “massive” the fanbase is. “I think I would have been very nervous if I had known how big it is,” she says.

Sunrise on the Reaping brought a lot of firsts for McCann, including shooting in a studio – the film shot at Germany’s Studio Babelsberg – and dying her hair. “I didn’t realize that when you dye your hair, you see yourself so differently,” she says. “I just thought it was the coolest thing ever.”

Director Francis Lawrence became, she says, an important creative ally during the shoot and she praises his collaborative approach and willingness to discuss scenes with the young cast. “He was always open for discussion, which made it great to know I could talk through things with him,” she says. “It really gave a sense of security while doing the scenes.”

The biggest challenge for McKenna while filming were the reaping scenes. McCann says she studied the previous films to note expressions on the faces of Katniss (Lawrence) and Prim (Willow Shields) when they were called to participate in the Games.

“It was challenging to get the look down that was scared but also controlled because you didn’t want the Capitol to see you scared at any point because you didn’t want to look weak to them,” she says. “Francis would always tell me to use my eyes and put it all through my eyes and keep it really contained while I acted. I found that was one of the most challenging things because I wanted to get it so right and for it to come across exactly how it did in the old movies. I wanted to carry that on and keep it looking correct.”

Up next, McCann can be seen in The Butler, an action comedy with Tom Hollander and Jean Reno from director Tom Edmunds, which she shot before Hunger Games. The film sees Reno plays a former WWI commando turned butler whose peaceful life is upended by mobsters collecting an old debt. McCann plays Harriett, a girl being looked after by him. While she admits she can’t reveal much yet, she says “it’s quite Christmassy with lots of action-packed moments.”

As for next steps, McCann says she’d love to do a musical one day. “If someone ever did a musical movie version of Beetlejuice, I would just love to be Lydia. I love Beetlejuice. I think it’s fantastic.”

#3331. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

Not everyone needs the company's most powerful models

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anthropic has a new AI model, and it's more powerful than the Claude most people are using for chat. And that's precisely why the company doesn't actually recommend switching to it for everyday tasks.

Claude Fable 5.2, released Monday alongside the more restricted Mythos 5.2, is designed for some of the toughest work AI can handle, including advanced coding, scientific research and complex engineering projects.

The timing is significant. Anthropic is also preparing for a massive initial public offering, putting fresh attention on how the company plans to turn increasingly powerful AI into a profitable business.

For Claude users, though, the immediate question is simpler: what can Fable 5.2 actually do, and is it worth using instead of Opus?

Fable 5.2 is designed for projects that require more than generating an email, summarizing a document or answering a question.

Anthropic says its newest model can handle complicated technical work that would otherwise require extensive human effort. During prerelease testing, its models helped engineers complete difficult software migrations, design working electronic devices and tackle advanced physics problems.

One of the more interesting applications is using Fable as an AI advisor. Rather than asking Fable to handle every task, developers can have smaller Claude models consult it when they encounter a particularly difficult problem.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Fable can also act as an orchestrator, coordinating smaller models and assigning them simpler tasks while it handles the more complicated work.

For everyday users, the most practical applications could include analyzing complex research, working through difficult technical problems or managing projects that involve multiple steps and large amounts of information.

Here's where Anthropic's lineup gets confusing. Despite introducing Fable 5.2 as one of its most capable models, Anthropic recommends that most people continue using Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday coding and knowledge work.

The company describes Opus as its strongest daily driver, while Fable is intended for more ambitious technical challenges. That means someone using Claude for writing, research, brainstorming or routine coding probably doesn't need to switch.

Fable becomes more interesting when a task requires sustained reasoning, complicated problem-solving or coordination between multiple AI systems.

There are also cheaper models in the lineup. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 remain options for simpler work where speed and efficiency matter more than maximum capability.

The takeaway is that the most powerful Claude isn't automatically the best Claude for every job.

Anthropic has reduced the price of Fable compared with its previous version, but it remains more expensive than Opus.

Through the API, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That's 20% less than Fable 5.1, although it's still twice the per-token price of Opus 5.5.

Anthropic also says the new model generates responses up to 30% faster than its predecessor. An optional fast mode offers even higher output speeds, but at twice the standard API token price.

For developers and businesses running large numbers of AI requests, those differences can add up quickly. If you run through your usage limits quickly, you might want to choose Opus 5.5 first.

For people using Claude through a subscription, access and usage limits also matter. Fable is available through supported Claude plans, although how much you can use depends on your subscription and any applicable usage credits.

Anthropic's latest model launch arrives at a particularly important moment for the company.

According to Reuters, Anthropic circulated IPO pricing information to banks before retracting it, saying the figures were inaccurate. The withdrawn proposal outlined a potential offering worth as much as $69.3 billion, although those numbers should not be treated as finalized.

The company is entering the public-market spotlight at a time when investors are scrutinizing the enormous cost of developing and operating advanced AI.

So, instead of offering one extremly powerful version of Claude for everyone, Anthropic is building a lineup designed for different types of work and different budgets.

Haiku and Sonnet can handle simpler, high-volume tasks. Opus serves as the everyday workhorse. Fable targets more demanding projects, while Mythos offers specialized capabilities to approved organizations working in fields such as cybersecurity and biomedical research.

It's a strategy that could help Anthropic serve more customers without requiring everyone to pay for its most expensive technology.

But it also creates a challenge: users need to understand why they should pay more for one model when another may already do everything they need.

As Anthropic moves toward its IPO, demonstrating that customers will pay for those additional capabilities could become just as important as achieving another impressive benchmark score.

If you're already using Claude Opus 5.5 for writing, research, brainstorming or everyday productivity, there's little reason to rush into Fable 5.2.

The new model is worth exploring if you're working on particularly difficult technical projects or tasks where existing AI models struggle to deliver reliable results.

For everyone else, Opus remains Anthropic's recommended starting point.
